claims.text: The initial nanoparticles contain five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios.
The initial nanoparticles are single-phase, homogeneous solid solutions.
High-entropy multimetal nanoparticle stability is governed by a balance between configurational entropy and reactive surface segregation.
Under inert thermoelectric conditions, high mixing entropy kinetically suppresses phase separation.
Under oxidizing catalytic conditions, the gas environment preferentially oxidizes certain constituent metals at nanoparticle surfaces.
Preferential surface oxidation triggers local compositional segregation.
Local compositional segregation causes structural instability.
Two otherwise identical nanoparticle batches will be thermally cycled from 473 to 1923 K, one under argon and one under a controlled oxidizing atmosphere.
Ramp rate, pressure, and sample handling are to be held constant between atmosphere treatments.
Metals with higher oxygen affinity oxidize preferentially at nanoparticle surfaces.
Selective oxidation lowers local mixing entropy.
Lower local mixing entropy promotes elemental segregation.
Oxidation-driven segregation produces secondary oxide phases and breaks down the initial solid solution.
After inert treatment, the nanoparticles will retain phase homogeneity by XRD and a uniform surface composition by XPS, with minimal change from the initial baseline.
After oxidizing treatment, the nanoparticles will exhibit detectable surface oxidation and emerging secondary-phase features.
Oxide peaks in XRD and altered oxidation states in XPS will indicate incipient phase segregation.
The onset temperature and extent of segregation depend on the oxidation affinities of the constituent metals and the reactive-gas conditions.
A lack of detectable differences in phase composition and surface oxidation between oxidizing and inert treatments would falsify the proposed atmosphere-driven segregation mechanism.
